newsitem.title: USA: AT&T's selection disappoints stock market.
newsitem.headline: AT&T's selection disappoints stock market.

text.p: AT&T Corp's selection of John Walter as successor to Chairman Robert Allen was greeted with some disappointment on Wall Street, and investors focused on a lengthy 18-month transition period for the change in leadership.

After a highly publicized search, the largest U.S. telephone company opted to go outside the phone industry and name Walter, chief executive of the commercial printing company R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co, as its new president and chief operating officer, effective November 1.
AT&T shares opened down 1-1/8 at 38-3/4 on Wednesday as investors scrambled to learn more about Walter.
Preliminary comments from Wall Street traders and analysts reflected concern that AT&T had bypassed some high-profile candidates with extensive telecommunications industry management experience.
"Perhaps the fact they had to go to an unknown in the telecommunications industry reflects a lack of interest by the knowns," said one Wall Street trader.
"John, who? " said David Goodtree, an industry analyst with Forrester Research.
"Does this mean AT&T is going back into the yellow pages?," Goodtree joked, referring to Donnelly's publishing of telephone directories.
Several analysts expressed concern about the extended transition period.

Walter will serve as AT&T president and chief operating officer for 15 months, take over as chief executive officer in January 1998, and add the post of chairman "at the AT&T annual meeting later that year," the company said. The annual meeting is usually held in April.
Several analysts expressed concern at the timing of the changes, which come in a period when AT&T must marshal its resources and workforce against an army of competitors.

AT&T is preparing to enter the local telephone business, even as the rival regional Bells enter long-distance markets. It also faces intense competition from upstart telecom firms that have nibbled away at its long-distance revenue base.

Citing these pressures, AT&T shocked Wall Street a month ago with a warning that its 1996 second half results would be disappointing. The warning sent AT&T's stock tumbling to new year-low trading levels, where it has essentially remained.

"This is an $80 billion company that has a great opportunity in front of it and is facing two of its biggest threats: deregulation and the Internet," Goodtree said. "So far it is not living up to expections. The guy (Walter) has got a big job to do."
Chicago Corp analyst Ken Leon said the selection of Walter only confirms his negative view of AT&T's stock. "I don't think it's going to go over well with investors," he said.
"Number one, (the choice of Walter) is outside the industry; and number two, (Donnelley) is not a company that is highly regarded for its management," Leon said.
He contrasted Donnelley with General Electric Co, a firm known for the quality and depth of its management.
